title: Unexpected stabilization of a single-$q$ charge density wave in pristine 1T-TiSe$_2$
authors: Kimoon Higashihira Han, Dongju Hwang, Dongsin Kim, Yeojin Ahn, Jaehun Cha, Seonggeon Gim, Gyubin Lee, Mingi Jho, Chan-young Lim, Sae Hee Ryu, Chris Jozwiak, Aaron Bostwick, Eli Rotenberg, Jonathan D. Denlinger, Makoto Hashimoto, Donghui Lu, Young Woo Choi, Gil Young Cho, Yeongkwan Kim
abstract: Over the past decade, studies revisiting the classical charge-density-wave system 1T-TiSe$_2$, long understood to host the $2 \times 2$ triple-$q$ order with equivalent subcomponents, have suggested that these subcomponents may not be identical, challenging a 50-year-old paradigm. Here, we demonstrate not only that these subcomponents are non-identical but also that they develop sequentially rather than simultaneously. By tracking folded-band features, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that a unidirectional $2 \times 1$ single-$q$ order stabilizes first, while the other two components emerge sequentially at lower temperatures, completing the triple-$q$ phase. Our free-energy analysis explains this hierarchy through repulsive coupling among the three subcomponents, as supported by first-principles calculations incorporating phonon anharmonicity. Consequently, the three subcomponents are inequivalent in both phase and amplitude. These results reconcile reported symmetry breaking and differing characteristic temperatures and establish a framework in which ostensibly simple, high-symmetry charge-density order emerges from temperature-dependent competition and cooperation among inequivalent subcomponents.
summary: This work reveals that the charge density wave (CDW) order in 1T-TiSe2 does not form simultaneously, contrary to previous beliefs. Using ARPES and free-energy theory, the authors demonstrate that the three CDW components condense sequentially due to repulsive coupling between them. This establishes a new framework for understanding complex, multi-component electronic order in correlated materials.
main_problem: The paper challenges the long-standing assumption that the three symmetry-related subcomponents of the CDW order in 1T-TiSe2 condense simultaneously into a single triple-q state.
main_result: The CDW order develops sequentially, starting with a unidirectional single-q component at the higher transition temperature, followed by the other two components at lower temperatures.
method: The study combines Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements with theoretical modeling, including free-energy analysis and first-principles calculations incorporating phonon anharmonicity.
model_or_system: The physical system is the layered transition-metal dichalcogenide 1T-TiSe2. The theoretical framework uses a Landau-Ginzburg free energy functional to model the competition between the three CDW subcomponents.
key_observables: Temperature-dependent spectral weight of folded bands measured by ARPES, and the relative amplitudes of the three CDW components.
important_parameters: The nature of the intercomponent coupling (repulsive vs. attractive) and the distinct transition temperatures ($T_{	ext{CDW}}$ and lower $T^*$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the sequential stabilization is governed by repulsive coupling among the three subcomponents, which is derived from free-energy minimization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature evolution of spectral weight at different high-symmetry points, constant-energy maps showing the sequential appearance of order, and phase diagrams contrasting attractive versus repulsive coupling scenarios.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by presenting ARPES evidence for the temperature-dependent condensation of the CDW components, followed by a theoretical explanation using free-energy analysis that establishes the repulsive interaction as the driving mechanism for sequential ordering.
why_interesting: The concept of sequential, competing order parameters driven by repulsive interactions is highly relevant to understanding complex phase transitions in strongly correlated electron systems, analogous to models in frustrated magnetism or orbital ordering.
